video_title: Ukraine's Lyman Offensive - Operation Vivaldi, Secrecy & How Lies can move Battlelines
gist: Perun analyses Ukraine's quietly run Operation Vivaldi counter-offensive by 3rd Army Corps north of Lyman, which apparently began in May 2026 and stayed hidden until September, alongside evidence of pervasive false reporting on the Russian side culminating in Putin's disproven claim to have captured Sviatohirsk. He cautions the outcome is unknown and draws lessons on opsec, drone tactics, reporting honesty and negotiation risk.

themes.theme: Operation Vivaldi and the Lyman salient

insights.claim: Ukraine's 3rd Army Corps has been counter-attacking the Russian salient north of Lyman in Donetsk under the name Operation Vivaldi, targeting Russia's 20th and 25th Combined Arms Armies, and Centre Group commander Biletskyi says it has several operational phases and is run under maximum information silence.
insights.speaker: host (Perun)
insights.so_what: A Ukrainian offensive initiative in the Donbas fortress-belt approaches undercuts the narrative of uniform Russian momentum.

insights.claim: Lyman matters because it is a road and rail crossroads: if Russia held it and the salient to its north, it could serve as a forward supply base and staging area against Slovyansk and Kramatorsk from the north, opening a possible pincer on the fortress belt.
insights.speaker: host (Perun)
insights.so_what: The fortress-belt cities anchor Ukraine's Donbas defence, so the Lyman salient is a key indicator of whether that line can hold.

insights.claim: In the drone-saturated war a supply road does not need to be physically occupied to become impassable, since fires and drones at close range are good enough, so a salient pressing towards Lyman threatens the lines of communication of the whole Slovyansk-Kramatorsk area.
insights.speaker: host (Perun)
insights.so_what: Territorial control lines understate how much ground is interdicted by fires, which matters when reading front-line maps.

insights.claim: Open-source reconstruction suggests Vivaldi began around late May 2026 with a mechanised assault on the salient's north after extensive drone preparation and Ukrainian electronic warfare, with Nove largely liberated by 1 June, yet DeepStateMap and pro-Russian maps still showed Nove under firm Russian control at the end of June and August.
insights.speaker: host (Perun)
insights.so_what: Public maps lagged the real front by months, so mapping-based trackers can miss operations until they are announced.

insights.claim: Glide-bomb strikes mapped by Clément Molin rose from about 71 in June to 152 in July in the salient area and their leading edge moved deeper each month, consistent with Ukrainian forces advancing (or being bombed as they advance) even while official maps showed no change.
insights.speaker: host (Perun)
insights.so_what: Russian air-strike patterns can act as an independent tell of where hidden Ukrainian advances are occurring.

insights.claim: Russian MoD weekly reports for the Zapad group in late August and September only said units 'improved the situation' or 'took more advantageous positions', with no claim of repelling a major attack.
insights.speaker: host (Perun)
insights.so_what: Vague MoD wording in a sector is a pattern signal that something unwelcome is happening there.
insights.quote: Units of the group improved the situation along the front lines.

insights.claim: Comparing three pre-Vivaldi and three during-Vivaldi weeks of Russian MoD claims, claimed Ukrainian armour losses fell from 50 to 35, artillery from 51 to 41 and motor vehicles from 374 to 336, with manpower up only about 10%, so Russian data show no sign of a costly major Ukrainian offensive.
insights.speaker: host (Perun)
insights.so_what: Either the offensive is cheap for Ukraine or Russian loss reporting is unreliable; both undermine attrition arguments against it.

insights.claim: Ukraine appears to have deliberately released old footage and slowed reporting to keep the media busy and hide the operation's true progress, and Biletskyi urged sources not to publish 'spoilers'.
insights.speaker: host (Perun)
insights.so_what: Ukrainian operational security in the information domain is functioning, so official silence should not be read as inactivity.

insights.claim: Visually confirmed Russian loss database LostArmour shows almost no recent geolocated Ukrainian vehicle losses in the salient: all boxed cases were from 2022-2025 except one June 2026 Humvee filmed from a Ukrainian car, suggesting Russian drone footage was not being posted or the Ukrainians were not being hit.
insights.speaker: host (Perun)
insights.so_what: Absence of Russian footage of kills is itself evidence about how much Russian commands knew or wanted to show.

insights.claim: Ukraine reportedly used its Unmanned Systems Forces model to shift punchy drone brigades (the 20th 'K-2' and 429th 'Achilles') to support 3rd Corps, whereas Russia mostly keeps drone units under Combined Arms Armies, trading unity of effort for less flexible reallocation.
insights.speaker: host (Perun)
insights.so_what: Organisational design of drone forces shapes who can mass effects at a chosen point of the front.

insights.claim: The Vivaldi offensive pattern is weeks of drone pressure establishing persistent observation and hunting artillery, logistics and communications to isolate positions, then an infantry push with armour and UGV support to clear, re-dig into tree lines or villages, reset and repeat.
insights.speaker: host (Perun)
insights.so_what: Shows that limited offensive manoeuvre is possible on a transparent battlefield if drone preparation is sufficiently long.

insights.claim: Ukraine claims 3rd Corps used heavy rotor drones to drop kamikaze ground robots deep behind Russian lines, and also engineering UGVs for remote mining, a 'Baneling drop' that pairs an expensive carrier with a cheap explosive payload.
insights.speaker: host (Perun)
insights.so_what: Signals rapid growth of ground-robot and heavy-drone demand and a shift of cost-exchange in Ukraine's favour.

insights.claim: Perun cautions that media 'firsts' in this war usually mean the first time something was reported, not the first time it was tried, which complicates the historical record and how analysts weigh claimed innovations.
insights.speaker: host (Perun)
insights.so_what: Treat announced 'world firsts' in battlefield tech with scepticism when sizing markets or capabilities.

themes.theme: Ukrainian command changes and Drapatyi's priorities

insights.claim: Ukraine has cycled through three Commanders-in-Chief (Zaluzhnyi, then Syrskyi, now Mykhailo Drapatyi) and four defence ministers; reformer Mykhailo Fedorov, appointed in January 2026, was de facto dropped in July after clashing with Syrskyi and publicly attacking him, and Syrskyi was removed shortly after.
insights.speaker: host (Perun)
insights.so_what: Leadership churn and political blowback in Kyiv are a risk factor for Ukrainian cohesion and Western confidence.

insights.claim: Russia by contrast is still on its second defence minister (Belousov replacing Shoigu) with Gerasimov unchanged as Chief of General Staff.
insights.speaker: host (Perun)
insights.so_what: Russian leadership stability despite poor performance points to a system that does not punish failure by turnover.

insights.claim: New commander-in-chief Drapatyi, a post-Soviet-generation officer who resigned in June 2025 after taking public responsibility for a missile strike that killed 12 troops at a training centre, is expected to favour accountability, mission command and learning faster than the enemy.
insights.speaker: host (Perun)
insights.so_what: His profile suggests a reforming, more aggressive Ukrainian command that seeks the initiative rather than only passive defence.

insights.claim: Drapatyi's eight objectives lead with stabilising the front while seizing the initiative where possible, and include reforming recruitment and rotation, unity of effort across services, faster tactical and technical innovation, and mission command in place of Soviet-style micromanagement.
insights.speaker: host (Perun)
insights.so_what: Explicit intent to attack selectively and to reform manning rules is a signpost for Ukraine's 2026-27 operational behaviour.

insights.claim: Open-source trackers show Russia's 2026 rate of advance far slower than 2025, closer to the late 2023 to early 2024 pace, as Ukrainian defensive reforms and counter-attacks bite and Russia concentrates in the heavily defended Donbas.
insights.speaker: host (Perun)
insights.so_what: A slowing Russian tempo weakens the case for imminent collapse of Ukrainian lines and shapes negotiation leverage.

insights.claim: Russian commentators complain that 'fine sounding reports' from commanders caused the Lyman situation, including the practice of reporting a position as taken in order to earn rewards and then rushing to actually capture it, called 'taking on credit'.
insights.speaker: host (Perun)
insights.so_what: Incentive structures that reward claimed rather than real gains degrade Russian command awareness.

insights.claim: False reporting is not only Russian: in late 2025 two Ukrainian brigade commanders were fired for falsely reporting troop presence near Siversk when positions were empty, allegedly aiding Russian capture, and Drapatyi devoted multiple paragraphs of his opening op-ed to honesty and to ending concealment of errors.
insights.speaker: host (Perun)
insights.so_what: Both sides face reporting integrity problems; the new Ukrainian commander is treating it as a priority.
insights.quote: Negligence and concealment of the truth are unacceptable.

insights.claim: The 2026 grey-zone battlefield makes false reporting easier than in 2022 because control of terrain is ambiguous, flags can be planted by drone and later destroyed, and AI-generated or recycled footage can now fake evidence of capture.
insights.speaker: host (Perun)
insights.so_what: Verification of battlefield claims is getting harder for analysts, markets and governments relying on public claims.

insights.claim: Perun's compounding-lies model holds that distortion grows with each layer up the chain, so the gap between Russian claimed control lines and even pro-Russian mapping has grown to thousands of square kilometres, for example a report to Putin that Russian forces were about 10 km from Sumy.
insights.speaker: host (Perun)
insights.so_what: Official Russian territorial claims should be heavily discounted when assessing war progress.

insights.claim: Perun argues front-line units and drone operators generally know reality, and evidence such as Russian glide-bomb strikes ordered at Group of Forces level on areas behind their own claimed lines suggests Russian commanders understood Ukrainians were present, but lacked the clarity or resources to deal with it.
insights.speaker: host (Perun)
insights.so_what: Russian operational awareness is likely better than the fully blind picture some bloggers describe, so reporting failures alone do not explain Lyman.

insights.claim: Perun cites a 2015 US Army War College paper, 'Lying to Ourselves', arguing officers lie because it is impossible to meet all imposed requirements, and notes that ghost soldiers in Yemen and Syria and rosy Afghanistan reporting show Western and other militaries are vulnerable too.
insights.speaker: host (Perun)
insights.so_what: Organisational incentives to tell superiors what they want to hear devalue expensive sensor and analysis systems.

insights.claim: AI tools can replicate human bad-reporting habits such as flattery and reluctance to say 'I don't know', so sensor and analysis networks may add a new source of distorted reporting to command chains.
insights.speaker: host (Perun)
insights.so_what: Analytic AI deployed in decision chains needs validation for sycophancy risk.

themes.theme: Putin's Sviatohirsk claim and the Kremlin information bubble

insights.claim: At the SCO meeting in Bishkek on 1 September 2026 Putin claimed 14 settlements captured in a month including Sviatohirsk, a city about 12 km behind the Ukrainian front line; RIA Novosti maps then changed to show it as Russian, and the MoD formally claimed it on 3 September, so reported reality was adjusted to fit the statement.
insights.speaker: host (Perun)
insights.so_what: Evidence that Russian official claims are being retrofitted to leader statements erodes their informational value.
insights.quote: Instead of a statement being adjusted to match reported reality, reported reality was being adjusted to match a statement.

insights.claim: Russian 'evidence' of capturing Sviatohirsk was a re-dubbed October 2025 Ukrainian video with the watermark removed, while Biletskyi posted a geolocated walk through the town on 7 September, and the Russian MoD still claimed on 19 September that clean-up of residential quarters continued.
insights.speaker: host (Perun)
insights.so_what: Doubling down on a disproven claim shows the Russian system does not self-correct publicly.

insights.claim: Perun says the Sviatohirsk lie makes little sense as pure information warfare, since it is easily disproved by high-information audiences and adds little for low-information ones, and considers it plausible that Putin's picture of the war is genuinely distorted, though he stresses uncertainty and that he is not a Kremlin whisperer.
insights.speaker: host (Perun)
insights.so_what: If Putin's view of the war is skewed, Russian willingness to accept realistic terms and the reaction to losses are harder to forecast.
insights.quote: the view of the war that Putin is getting from his seat doesn't fully align with reality

insights.claim: Colonel General Sergey Kuzovlev, commander of the Zapad Grouping, received a Hero of the Russian Federation medal in December 2025 after claiming the capture of Kupyansk, which Ukraine contradicted with video of Zelenskyy visiting, illustrating the incentive to exaggerate gains.
insights.speaker: host (Perun)
insights.so_what: Promotion and medal incentives reward overclaiming, so Russian command reports should be treated as biased upward.

insights.claim: Digital manipulation is used by both sides: Ukraine's 425th Assault Regiment was reported in December 2025 to have altered footage to replace Russian flags with Ukrainian ones.
insights.speaker: host (Perun)
insights.so_what: Information-warfare tooling is cheap and symmetric, so unverified battlefield video should be treated with caution.

themes.theme: Implications for negotiations and other militaries

insights.claim: If Ukraine and its allies see a Lyman counter-attack while the Kremlin is told Russian troops are hunting Biletskyi through Sviatohirsk basements, the lack of shared factual ground lowers the odds of a settlement both sides consider fair, so Ukrainian battlefield success may paradoxically make peace harder.
insights.speaker: host (Perun)
insights.so_what: Negotiation timelines may be longer than battlefield trends imply if Moscow's perception lags reality.
insights.quote: the odds of actually getting an agreement that both sides consider fair potentially goes down

insights.claim: Vivaldi shows that operational security is still possible in an era of drones and satellites and that some offensive manoeuvre is feasible on a Ukraine-style battlefield, lessons other militaries will absorb.
insights.speaker: host (Perun)
insights.so_what: Doctrine and procurement shifts toward deception, drone preparation and UGVs are likely across NATO militaries.

insights.claim: Perun cautions Vivaldi's outcome is unknown: Russia still pushes elsewhere, Ukrainian casualty and manning shortfalls are a critical concern, long-range strike campaigns continue as winter approaches, and Ukraine has said it would accept an energy, Black Sea or general ceasefire.
insights.speaker: host (Perun)
insights.so_what: Balanced view: one local success does not change the wider attritional and manpower picture.

insights.claim: Perun reports that a CIA chief's recent Moscow visit has been characterised in some sources as an attempt to pierce the Russian information bubble, though the sourcing is anonymous and he does not know the truth.
insights.speaker: host (Perun)
insights.so_what: Signals US engagement on giving Moscow a realistic battlefield assessment, but weakly sourced.
